scenario.briefing: A game studio's score feed may include nil gaps. Summarize every argument without silently truncating the list.

title: Varargs and multiple returns
summary: Count and sum variadic arguments, then repair a summary that loses values after the first nil.

objectives.description: Use select to count and read variadic arguments.
Find a table pack that drops values after nil.
Select one variadic argument by position.

hints: select(index, ...) returns the values starting at that position.
Parentheses keep one value from a multiple return.
Return both the count and the total.

misconceptions.description: Using the length of a packed table to count varargs.
misconceptions.feedback: The # operator counts a sequence until its first nil. select("#", ...) counts every argument, including nil holes.

misconceptions.description: Packing varargs into a table and losing values after nil.
misconceptions.feedback: A table constructor stops at the first nil hole, and ipairs stops there too. Iterate by index up to select("#", ...) instead.

misconceptions.description: Returning only the total and dropping the count.
misconceptions.testDescription: The function counts and sums every argument.
misconceptions.feedback: Multiple returns are part of the contract. Return count, total so callers can read either value.

misconceptions.diagnostic: Adding select(index, ...) to total without a nil fallback, so one gap raises an arithmetic error.
misconceptions.feedback: A nil gap is still an argument. Default it to zero before adding, or define the policy for missing scores explicitly.

sections.title: Functions can return several values
sections.body: A Lua function returns a list: return count, total. A caller can capture both, ignore the second, or keep only the first. An extra value is discarded, and a missing value becomes nil. When a call is not the last expression in a list, only its first result is used.

sections.title: Varargs are a list, not a table
sections.body: A function declared as function stats(...) receives every extra argument. select("#", ...) returns how many there are. select(index, ...) returns all values from index onward; wrapped in parentheses, it yields just that one value. A table constructor such as { ... } stops at the first nil, so it is not a reliable pack for sparse arguments.

sections.title: Choose one representation
sections.body: Multiple returns are convenient for a count and a total. A table is better when the caller must store the values or pass them on later. When a nil is meaningful, build the table by index with select and keep an explicit length. Document which representation the function promises.

steps.title: Count and sum the score feed
steps.prompt: Edit main.lua. stats returns how many arguments it received and their sum, treating nil as zero.
hints: Default a nil gap to zero before adding.

files.content:
local function stats(...)
  local count = 0
  local total = 0
  for _, value in ipairs({ ... }) do
    total = total + value
  end
  return count, total
end

local count, total = stats(3, nil, 2)
print(count, total)

localVerification.description: Runs the file with the Lua interpreter and prints the count and total.

tests.description: The function returns both a count and a total.
The function counts and sums every argument.

steps.title: The summary stops at the gap
steps.prompt: A score feed with a nil gap reports only the values before the gap. Select the faulty instruction and the correct repair.
hints: The values arrive as varargs, not as a ready sequence.
A table constructor stops at the first nil.
ipairs also stops at the first nil.
Use select("#", ...) and an index loop.

fixes.label: Use select("#", ...) and iterate indexes with select(index, ...).
Use #values to recover the missing length.

steps.explanation: The table constructor and ipairs both stop at the nil, so later values never reach the loop. select("#", ...) preserves the true count, and select(index, ...) reads each position.

steps.title: Read one vararg
steps.prompt: Inside a variadic function, which expression returns only the third argument?
hints: select(n, ...) returns values starting at n.
The parentheses matter when one value is needed.

quiz.prompt: Inside a variadic function, which expression returns only the third argument?
quiz.explanation: select(3, ...) starts at the third argument, and the parentheses keep a single value. The # operator needs a table, and arg is not an implicit vararg table.
